s: Rewards meant to solve a problem can sometimes make it worse.
A well-known story from colonial Delhi tells of a bounty paid for every dead cobra, which led some residents to start breeding cobras for the reward.
When officials discovered the trick and cancelled the scheme, the breeders released their now worthless snakes, leaving more cobras than before.
Historians doubt that the story happened as told, but economists still use the name 'cobra effect' for any incentive that rewards the wrong behaviour.
marks: Rewards meant to solve a problem
cues: States the general claim without pointing back to anything.
Gives the story that illustrates the claim.
'The trick' is the breeding just described, and the scheme must exist before it can be cancelled.
Comments on the whole story and names the effect, so it closes the paragraph.
odd: Cobras are among the most venomous snakes in South Asia, and their bites remain a serious danger in rural areas.
oddWhy: It is about cobras as a danger, not about rewards that backfire.
ins: For a while the scheme seemed to work, as officials kept paying out for dead snakes.
insWhy: 'The scheme' needs the bounty from the second sentence, and 'for a while' must come before officials discover the trick.

sum.t: Incentives can backfire by rewarding the very behaviour they target, as a doubtful but telling story about cobra bounties shows.
sum.why: Covers the general claim, the example and the doubt about the story.

sum.t: Residents of colonial Delhi bred cobras to collect a bounty.
sum.why: Only the example, without the point it illustrates.

sum.t: Every reward offered by a government ends up making the original problem worse, which is why economists oppose bounties of any kind.
sum.why: The paragraph says rewards 'can sometimes' backfire, and no one is said to oppose all bounties.

sum.t: Historians have proved that the cobra story is false, so the cobra effect is not a real idea.
sum.why: Historians doubt the story, but economists still use the idea.

s: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill.
Doctors long assumed that it could help only if patients believed it was real medicine.
That assumption has been challenged by trials of so-called open-label placebos, in which patients are told plainly that their pills contain nothing active.
In several such studies, people with conditions like irritable bowel syndrome still reported feeling better, though researchers disagree about why.
cues: Defines the term the rest of the paragraph uses.
'It' refers to the placebo just defined.
'That assumption' points back to the belief in the second sentence.
'Such studies' are the open-label trials just introduced.
odd: Some modern medicines began as plant remedies, such as quinine, which comes from the bark of the cinchona tree.
oddWhy: It is about where real drugs come from, not about placebos working without deception.
ins: In one trial, the pills even came in a bottle labelled 'placebo pills'.
insWhy: It adds a detail of how the open-label trials were run, so it follows their description and comes before the results.

sum.t: Placebos may help even when patients know they are inert, which challenges an old assumption, though the reason is unclear.
sum.why: Covers the old view, the challenge and the open question.

sum.t: Patients with irritable bowel syndrome felt better after taking pills with nothing active in them.
sum.why: One finding, without the old assumption it challenges.

sum.t: Open-label trials have proved that belief plays no part in how any treatment works, so doctors can now replace most real medicines with honest placebos.
sum.why: The studies are few, the reason is disputed, and nothing suggests replacing real medicine.

sum.t: Doctors were right that placebos work only when patients are deceived.
sum.why: The trials challenge exactly that belief.

s: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable metal type in the German city of Mainz.
Within fifty years, presses were running in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced.
This flood of cheap print did more than spread existing texts.
It also encouraged writing in everyday languages rather than Latin, since printers wanted to sell to as many readers as possible.
cues: Introduces Gutenberg and the date, so it opens.
'Within fifty years' counts from the date in the first sentence.
'This flood' sums up the millions of books just mentioned.
'It also' completes 'did more than', naming the further effect.
odd: Paper had reached Europe from China through the Islamic world several centuries earlier.
oddWhy: It is about how paper arrived centuries before, not about the spread and effects of printing.
ins: His press could produce many copies of a page in the time a scribe needed to copy one by hand.
insWhy: 'His press' needs Gutenberg named just before it, and the speed it describes explains the rapid spread that follows.

sum.t: Gutenberg's press spread quickly across Europe and, by making print cheap, also pushed writing towards everyday languages.
sum.why: Covers the invention, its spread and its further effect.

sum.t: Gutenberg began printing with movable type in Mainz around 1450.
sum.why: Only the opening fact.

sum.t: Printing ended the use of Latin across Europe and left every scribe without work within a few years of Gutenberg's first books.
sum.why: The paragraph says print encouraged everyday languages, not that Latin vanished; scribes are not discussed.

sum.t: Printers preferred Latin because it let them sell books across the whole of Europe.
sum.why: The paragraph says the opposite: printers chose everyday languages to reach more readers.

s: In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin argued that resources shared by everyone are bound to be ruined.
If a pasture is open to all, he reasoned, each herder gains by adding another animal, while the cost of overgrazing is spread across the whole village.
The political scientist Elinor Ostrom later showed that this outcome is far from inevitable.
Studying fisheries, forests and irrigation systems around the world, she found many communities that had managed shared resources well for generations through rules they made and enforced themselves.
marks: this outcome is far from inevitable
cues: Names Hardin and states his claim, so it opens.
'He reasoned' refers to Hardin and spells out his argument.
'Later' and 'this outcome' answer Hardin's prediction.
'She' is Ostrom, and the sentence gives her evidence.
odd: Hardin also wrote widely about population growth, which he saw as a threat to the planet.
oddWhy: It is about Hardin's other views, not about whether shared resources must be ruined.
ins: Hardin called this logic, in which each sensible choice adds up to collective ruin, the tragedy of the commons.
insWhy: 'This logic' of individual choices adding up to ruin is the herder reasoning, so it follows that sentence and comes before Ostrom's reply.

sum.t: Hardin held that self-interest dooms shared resources, but Ostrom found communities that manage them well with their own rules.
sum.why: Covers both views and the evidence against Hardin.

sum.t: Herders gain by adding animals to a pasture that everyone shares.
sum.why: Only one step of Hardin's argument.

sum.t: Ostrom proved that shared resources are always managed well when local people are left alone.
sum.why: She found many well-managed cases, not that it always works.

sum.t: Governments should hand every forest and fishery over to local communities.
sum.why: No policy is recommended.

s: Economists advise that decisions should depend on future costs and benefits, not on money already spent.
Money that cannot be recovered, which they call a sunk cost, should not affect what you do next.
People find this advice surprisingly hard to follow.
Someone who has paid for a concert ticket will often go out in a storm to attend, even when they would rather stay home, simply because the ticket was expensive.
marks: decisions should depend on future costs
which they call a sunk cost
Someone who has paid for a concert ticket
cues: States the economists' advice, so it opens.
'They' are the economists, and the sentence names the idea.
'This advice' points back to the advice in the first two sentences.
Gives an example of people failing to follow the advice.
odd: Ticket prices for big concerts have risen in many countries, partly because artists now earn less from selling recordings.
oddWhy: It is about why tickets cost more, not about letting past spending shape decisions.
ins: The same reasoning keeps failing projects alive, because abandoning them feels like wasting what has already been spent.
insWhy: 'The same reasoning' needs the concert example before it, so it comes last.

sum.t: Past spending should not guide future choices, yet people find it hard to ignore money already spent.
sum.why: Covers the advice and the difficulty of following it.

sum.t: People go to concerts in bad weather because their tickets were expensive.
sum.why: Only the example.

sum.t: Economists say people should not think about costs at all when they decide how to spend their money, whether the money is already spent or not.
sum.why: Only money already spent should be ignored; future costs still count.

sum.t: Everyone who buys an expensive ticket will attend the event, whatever the weather or their mood.
sum.why: The paragraph says 'often', not everyone.

s: In the 1990s the anthropologist Robin Dunbar noticed that primates with a larger neocortex tend to live in larger groups.
Extending the pattern to humans, he estimated that people can keep up stable relationships with about 150 others.
The figure, now known as Dunbar's number, has been used to plan army units, villages and even company departments.
Critics, however, argue that the estimate rests on shaky statistics and that the number of relationships people manage varies widely.
marks: The figure, now known as Dunbar's number
cues: Introduces Dunbar and his observation, so it opens.
'The pattern' is the link between brain and group size just described.
'The figure' is the 150 just estimated.
'However' turns from the number's uses to doubts about it.
odd: Chimpanzees spend a large part of each day grooming one another, which helps keep their alliances strong.
oddWhy: It is about how chimpanzees bond, not about the number of human relationships or doubts about it.
ins: That is roughly the size of a hunter-gatherer clan or a traditional village, he pointed out.
insWhy: 'That' is the figure of 150 just given, and the comparison supports it before the uses and doubts that follow.

sum.t: Dunbar's estimate that people can sustain about 150 relationships has been widely applied, though critics question its basis.
sum.why: Covers the estimate, its use and the criticism.

sum.t: Primates with a larger neocortex tend to live in larger groups.
sum.why: Only the starting observation.

sum.t: Because the human brain cannot handle more than 150 relationships, every organisation should be split into groups of exactly that size.
sum.why: The paragraph neither states a hard limit nor gives advice.

sum.t: Critics have shown that people keep far more than 150 relationships, so Dunbar's research has been abandoned.
sum.why: Critics question the statistics and note variation; nothing says the idea was abandoned.

s: Tulip mania in the Dutch Republic of the 1630s is often told as the first great financial bubble.
In the familiar version, prices for rare bulbs rose to the cost of a house before collapsing in early 1637, ruining thousands of investors.
The historian Anne Goldgar, working through Dutch archives, found little evidence of such widespread ruin.
The trade, she argued, involved a fairly small circle of merchants and craftsmen, and the crash caused embarrassment and disputes rather than economic disaster.
marks: is often told as the first great financial bubble
found little evidence of such widespread ruin
cues: Introduces the episode and its usual reputation, so it opens.
'The familiar version' spells out how the story is usually told.
'Such widespread ruin' points back to the ruined investors.
'She' is Goldgar, and the sentence gives her alternative account.
odd: Tulips had arrived in Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century.
oddWhy: It is about where tulips came from, not about whether the mania was as ruinous as told.
ins: If she is right, the most famous bubble in history says more about the power of a good story than about markets.
insWhy: 'If she is right' needs Goldgar's whole argument, which ends in the last sentence, and it draws the conclusion.

sum.t: Tulip mania is remembered as a ruinous bubble, but archival research suggests its scale and damage were exaggerated.
sum.why: Covers the usual story and the challenge to it.

sum.t: Prices for rare tulip bulbs collapsed in early 1637.
sum.why: Only one detail of the usual story.

sum.t: Tulip mania never happened; the story was invented by historians who wanted a warning against greed.
sum.why: Goldgar questions the scale of the ruin, not that the trade and crash happened.

sum.t: Financial bubbles do far less harm than economists believe, as the history of markets from the Dutch tulip trade of the 1630s to the present shows.
sum.why: The paragraph is about one episode and makes no claim about bubbles in general.

s: In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus spent years memorising lists of nonsense syllables and testing himself on them.
He found that a large part of what he learned was lost within the first day, after which forgetting slowed down.
He also found that each review made the memory last longer than the one before.
This is why spacing out reviews over days and weeks works better than cramming the same hours into one night.
marks: He found that a large part
This is why spacing out reviews
cues: Introduces Ebbinghaus and his experiment, so it opens.
'He found' gives the first result of the experiment.
'Also' marks the second finding, so it follows the first.
'This is why' draws the practical lesson from the second finding.
odd: Nonsense syllables such as 'DAX' or 'BOK' are still used in some memory experiments today.
oddWhy: It is about the test material, not about how memories fade and how reviews help.
ins: He chose nonsense syllables so that meaning and earlier knowledge could not help him remember.
insWhy: It explains the method in the first sentence, so it follows it and comes before the results.

sum.t: Ebbinghaus showed that memories fade fast at first but last longer with each review, which is why spaced study beats cramming.
sum.why: Covers both findings and the lesson drawn from them.

sum.t: Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables in the 1880s.
sum.why: Only the method.

sum.t: Anything learned once is forgotten within a day unless it is reviewed every single night, which is why Ebbinghaus tested himself daily for years.
sum.why: The paragraph says a large part is lost, not everything, and recommends spacing reviews out, not reviewing nightly.

sum.t: Schools should replace exams with weekly quizzes spread across the year.
sum.why: No advice to schools is given.

s: Writing is often imagined as an invention for recording stories, laws or prayers.
In Mesopotamia, where some of the earliest writing appears, the oldest clay tablets tell a humbler tale.
Most of them, dating from around 3200 BCE in the city of Uruk, are records of grain, livestock, beer and labour kept by temple administrators.
Only centuries later did scribes begin to use the same marks to write down literature, letters and royal boasts.
marks: the oldest clay tablets tell a humbler tale
cues: States the common view that the rest corrects, so it opens.
'A humbler tale' contrasts with the grand uses just listed.
'Most of them' refers to the oldest tablets.
'Only centuries later' looks back from the earliest records.
odd: Clay was plentiful in Mesopotamia, while stone and timber had to be brought from far away.
oddWhy: It is about building materials, not about what the earliest writing recorded.
ins: Many of their signs began as simple pictures of the things being counted, such as a sheaf of grain or a jar of oil.
insWhy: 'Their signs' are the administrators' records just described, and pictures of counted goods come before the later move to literature.

sum.t: The earliest Mesopotamian writing mostly kept administrative accounts; its use for literature and letters came much later.
sum.why: Covers the correction to the common view and the later development.

sum.t: Temple administrators in Uruk recorded grain, beer and labour on clay tablets.
sum.why: Only the evidence, without the point it makes.

sum.t: Writing has always been used mainly for accounting, and literature has never mattered much to any civilisation that used it.
sum.why: The paragraph is about how writing began, not about all of history.

sum.t: Mesopotamian scribes invented writing in order to preserve their religious stories and laws.
sum.why: This is the common view that the paragraph corrects.

topic: When a new road slows traffic
s: In 1968 the mathematician Dietrich Braess showed that adding a road to a network can make every driver's journey slower.
The reason is that each driver picks the route that is fastest for themselves, without regard to the delay they cause others.
So a new shortcut can lure so many cars that it clogs the roads feeding it, leaving everyone worse off than before it was built.
The reverse has also been observed: when Seoul removed a busy elevated road, traffic in the area did not get worse as many had feared.
marks: The reason is that each driver
So a new shortcut can lure
The reverse has also been observed
cues: States Braess's finding, so it opens.
'The reason' explains the surprising finding just stated.
'So' draws the consequence of each driver's selfish choice.
'The reverse' needs the case of adding a road before it.
odd: Traffic engineers now use computer models to time traffic lights across whole districts.
oddWhy: It is about timing lights, not about how adding or removing roads changes traffic.
ins: The result is now known as Braess's paradox.
insWhy: 'The result' is the finding in the first sentence, which it names before the explanation begins.

sum.t: Because drivers choose routes selfishly, adding a road can slow traffic for everyone, and removing one need not make it worse.
sum.why: Covers the finding, its cause and the reverse case.

sum.t: Seoul removed a busy road without making traffic worse.
sum.why: Only the last example.

sum.t: Building new roads always increases congestion, so every city should remove its busiest roads, as Seoul did, to cure its traffic jams for good.
sum.why: The paragraph says a new road 'can' slow traffic, and gives no advice.

sum.t: Braess showed that traffic jams are caused by drivers who choose slow routes on purpose.
sum.why: Drivers choose the fastest route for themselves; the problem is the effect on others.

s: Reef-building corals depend on tiny algae that live inside their tissues and supply them with food made by photosynthesis.
When the water stays too warm for too long, this partnership breaks down and the corals expel the algae.
Without them the corals turn white, which is why the process is called bleaching.
Bleached corals are not yet dead, and they can recover if temperatures fall quickly, but repeated heatwaves give them little time to do so.
marks: Without them the corals turn white
Bleached corals are not yet dead
cues: Introduces the corals and their algae, so it opens.
'This partnership' is the coral and algae relationship just described.
'Them' are the expelled algae.
'Bleached' needs the process named just before.
odd: Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor but are home to a large share of marine species.
oddWhy: It is about how rich reefs are, not about how and why corals bleach.
ins: The expelled algae take most of the coral's colour with them.
insWhy: It needs the algae to have been expelled, and it explains why the corals then turn white.

sum.t: Prolonged heat makes corals expel the algae they rely on, and while bleached corals can recover, frequent heatwaves leave little time.
sum.why: Covers the cause, the process and the chance of recovery.

sum.t: Corals turn white when they lose their algae.
sum.why: Only one step of the process.

sum.t: Any rise in sea temperature kills coral reefs at once.
sum.why: Bleaching follows prolonged heat, and bleached corals are not yet dead.

sum.t: Bleaching happens when algae feed on the coral's tissues during warm weather.
sum.why: The algae supply food to the coral; heat makes the coral expel them.

s: When coins were made of precious metal, their value depended partly on how much metal they contained.
If worn or clipped coins circulated at the same official value as full-weight ones, people had a reason to spend the light coins and keep the heavy ones.
Before long, only the light coins were seen in everyday trade, while the good ones were hoarded, melted down or sent abroad.
This tendency came to be called Gresham's law, after a sixteenth-century English financier, and is summed up in the phrase 'bad money drives out good'.
marks: Before long, only the light coins
This tendency came to be called
cues: Sets out how coin value worked, so it opens.
Applies that idea to light and full-weight coins.
'Before long' gives the result of people spending light coins.
'This tendency' names the pattern just described.
odd: Gold coins were also prized for their beauty, and many were kept as jewellery or given as gifts.
oddWhy: It is about coins as ornaments, not about light coins replacing good ones.
ins: The law holds only when both kinds of money must be accepted at the same value; where people can price coins freely, good money tends to win instead.
insWhy: 'The law' needs Gresham's law named first, and the sentence adds a limit to it, so it comes last.

sum.t: If light and full-weight coins must pass at one value, people spend the light ones and hoard the rest: Gresham's law.
sum.why: Covers the mechanism and the name.

sum.t: Gresham was a sixteenth-century English financier.
sum.why: Only a detail about the name.

sum.t: Bad money always replaces good money in every economy and every period of history, whatever the rules that fix its value.
sum.why: The law depends on coins having to pass at the same value.

sum.t: Governments should stop making coins from precious metals to prevent hoarding.
sum.why: No advice is given.

s: In the 1920s and 1930s, researchers at the Hawthorne Works, a factory near Chicago, studied how working conditions affected output.
In some of their experiments, productivity seemed to rise whatever they changed, whether the lights were made brighter or dimmer.
This led to the idea of the Hawthorne effect: people work differently simply because they know they are being watched.
Later reanalyses of the original data, however, found the evidence for this effect much weaker and messier than the textbook story suggests.
cues: Introduces the studies, so it opens.
'Their experiments' are the studies just introduced.
'This' is the puzzling rise in productivity.
'Later' and 'however' challenge the idea just named.
odd: Western Electric, which owned the factory, made telephone equipment for the Bell system.
oddWhy: It is about the company, not about the studies or the effect named after them.
ins: Even so, the term remains a useful warning that observing people can change what they do.
insWhy: 'Even so' concedes the weak evidence in the last sentence, so it must come after it.

sum.t: Factory studies gave rise to the idea that being watched changes how people work, though later analyses found the evidence weak.
sum.why: Covers the studies, the idea and the doubt.

sum.t: Output at the Hawthorne factory rose when the lights were made brighter.
sum.why: One result, and only half of it.

sum.t: The Hawthorne effect has been disproved, so researchers no longer need to worry that observing people affects them.
sum.why: The evidence is weaker, not disproved.

sum.t: Workers always become more productive when managers watch them closely, as every study of factory work since the 1920s has confirmed beyond doubt.
sum.why: Later reanalyses found the evidence weak.

s: Until the 1950s, loading a cargo ship meant carrying sacks, barrels and crates aboard one by one.
In 1956 the American trucking businessman Malcom McLean sent a ship from New Jersey to Texas carrying goods packed in large steel boxes.
The boxes could be lifted straight from trucks or trains onto ships and off again, without ever being unpacked.
As this method spread, the cost and time of moving goods by sea fell sharply, helping to make global supply chains possible.
cues: Describes the old way, so it opens.
The date and the new idea follow the description of the old way.
'The boxes' are the steel boxes just introduced.
'This method' is the box system just described.
odd: Air freight, though faster, still carries only a small share of world trade by weight.
oddWhy: It is about air freight, not about how containers changed shipping.
ins: The work was slow and costly, and a ship could spend days in port being loaded.
insWhy: 'The work' is the loading by hand in the first sentence, so it follows it, before the new idea.

sum.t: Shipping goods in standard steel boxes that move between trucks, trains and ships cut costs sharply and helped globalise trade.
sum.why: Covers the old way, the innovation and its effect.

sum.t: Malcom McLean sent a ship of steel boxes from New Jersey to Texas in 1956.
sum.why: Only the first voyage.

sum.t: Containers made sea transport almost free and soon replaced every other way of moving goods, from railways and lorries to aircraft, around the world.
sum.why: Costs fell sharply; nothing says they vanished or that other transport ended.

sum.t: Containers made loading slower at first, because each box had to be unpacked at every port.
sum.why: The boxes were moved without being unpacked.

s: Our galaxy contains hundreds of billions of stars, many of them far older than the Sun.
If even a small fraction had planets where intelligent life arose, some civilisations should have had time to spread across the galaxy.
Yet we see no clear sign of anyone else.
This puzzle, often credited to the physicist Enrico Fermi, has many proposed answers, from the rarity of life to the possibility that civilisations destroy themselves.
marks: Yet we see no clear sign
cues: Sets out the size and age of the galaxy, so it opens.
'A small fraction' is of the stars just mentioned.
'Yet' sets the silence against the expectation just raised.
'This puzzle' is the clash between expectation and silence.
odd: Astronomers measure the distances to nearby stars by watching how their positions shift as the Earth orbits the Sun.
oddWhy: It is about measuring distances, not about the missing civilisations.
ins: Even at a small fraction of the speed of light, a civilisation could cross the galaxy in a few tens of millions of years, a blink in its long history.
insWhy: It backs up 'had time to spread' in the second sentence, before 'Yet' turns to the silence.

sum.t: Given the galaxy's size and age, other civilisations should be visible, and why none is seen remains an open puzzle.
sum.why: Covers the expectation, the silence and the open question.

sum.t: Many stars in our galaxy are older than the Sun.
sum.why: Only the starting fact.

sum.t: The absence of signals proves that humans are the only intelligent life in the universe, so the search for other civilisations should end.
sum.why: The paragraph lists many possible answers; it proves nothing.

sum.t: Governments should spend more on searching for signals from other civilisations.
sum.why: No advice is given.

s: An ancient puzzle asks about the ship of the Greek hero Theseus, preserved by the Athenians for centuries.
As its planks rotted, they were replaced one at a time, until none of the original wood remained.
Was it still the same ship?
The philosopher Thomas Hobbes sharpened the question by asking what we should say if someone had kept the old planks and built a second ship from them.
marks: Was it still the same ship?
cues: Introduces the puzzle, so it opens.
'Its planks' are the ship's.
The question follows the full replacement just described.
'The question' is the one just asked, which Hobbes made harder.
odd: Theseus was said to have killed the Minotaur in the labyrinth of Crete.
oddWhy: It is about Theseus's legend, not about the identity of his ship.
ins: Now there would be two ships with a claim to the name, and each claim seems strong.
insWhy: 'Two ships' needs the rebuilt second ship from the last sentence.

sum.t: The ship of Theseus asks whether an object survives the replacement of all its parts, a puzzle Hobbes deepened with a rebuilt rival.
sum.why: Covers the puzzle and Hobbes's twist.

sum.t: The Athenians kept Theseus's ship for centuries.
sum.why: Only a detail of the story.

sum.t: Hobbes solved the puzzle by showing that the rebuilt ship was the real one.
sum.why: Hobbes sharpened the question; he did not settle it here.

sum.t: Philosophers agree that nothing keeps its identity over time, since all objects change their parts.
sum.why: No such agreement is mentioned.

s: In nineteenth-century France, the official Salon in Paris largely decided which painters could build a career.
Its juries favoured polished historical and mythological scenes, and they often rejected work that looked sketchy or unfinished.
In 1874 a group of painters frustrated by the Salon, including Monet, Renoir and Degas, put on an exhibition of their own.
A critic mocked one of Monet's paintings, Impression, Sunrise, and the name 'Impressionists' stuck.
marks: A critic mocked one of Monet's paintings
cues: Introduces the Salon, so it opens.
'Its juries' are the Salon's.
The painters' own show responds to the Salon's tastes.
The critic reacts to the exhibition, and Monet is already named.
odd: Paris was rebuilt with wide boulevards in the 1850s and 1860s under Baron Haussmann.
oddWhy: It is about rebuilding Paris, not about the Salon and the painters it rejected.
ins: Their verdict mattered, because painters who were refused often struggled to find buyers.
insWhy: 'Their verdict' is the juries' judgement just described, and it explains why rejection pushed the painters to act.

sum.t: Shut out by the Salon's taste, a group of painters exhibited on their own in 1874 and took their name from a critic's jibe.
sum.why: Covers the Salon, the independent show and the name.

sum.t: A critic mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise.
sum.why: Only the last event.

sum.t: The Salon praised the Impressionists' sketchy style and invited them to exhibit in 1874.
sum.why: The Salon disliked sketchy work, and the painters exhibited on their own.

sum.t: The Salon rejected every painter of the age, which is why all the great artists of the nineteenth century ended up joining the Impressionists.
sum.why: The Salon 'often' rejected certain work; nothing says all artists became Impressionists.

s: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mould growing on one of his culture plates had killed the bacteria around it.
He named the substance it produced penicillin, but he struggled to purify it and soon turned to other work.
A decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford took up the problem and showed that purified penicillin could cure infections in mice and then in people.
By the end of the Second World War it was being mass-produced, and Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.
marks: By the end of the Second World War
cues: Gives the discovery and its date, so it opens.
'He' is Fleming, and 'it' is the mould.
'A decade later' counts from Fleming's work, and 'the problem' is purifying it.
Follows the medical tests with mass production and the prize.
odd: Bacteria are single-celled organisms, and most of them are harmless to people.
oddWhy: It is about bacteria in general, not about how penicillin became a medicine.
ins: Their first human patient, a policeman, improved at first but died when the supply ran out.
insWhy: 'Their' refers to Florey and Chain, and the patient belongs to their tests on people, before mass production.

sum.t: Fleming discovered penicillin by chance, but Florey and Chain's later work turned it into a usable medicine.
sum.why: Covers the discovery and the work that made it a drug.

sum.t: Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.
sum.why: Only the last fact.

sum.t: Fleming purified penicillin himself and tested it successfully on his own patients within months of his chance discovery in 1928.
sum.why: Fleming struggled to purify it; Florey and Chain did that a decade later.

sum.t: Penicillin was useless until the war, and Fleming deserved no credit at all for discovering it.
sum.why: He shared the Nobel Prize; the paragraph does not deny him credit.

s: Textbooks often warn that people in a crowd are less likely to help a stranger in trouble.
The idea, known as the bystander effect, comes from laboratory studies in which participants were slower to respond to an emergency when others were present.
A 2019 study took a different approach, analysing CCTV footage of real public conflicts in three countries.
In nine out of ten cases, at least one bystander stepped in, and the more people were present, the more likely someone was to help.
marks: A 2019 study took a different approach
In nine out of ten cases
cues: States the common warning, so it opens.
'The idea' is the warning just stated, and the sentence gives its source.
'A different approach' contrasts with the laboratory studies.
Gives the results of the 2019 study.
odd: Many cities have expanded their CCTV networks in recent decades, raising concerns about privacy.
oddWhy: It is about surveillance, not about whether bystanders help.
ins: This does not mean each person in a crowd is more likely to act, only that someone usually does.
insWhy: 'This' is the finding about larger crowds in the last sentence, which it qualifies.

sum.t: Lab studies suggest crowds make people slow to help, but real footage shows that someone usually steps in, more often in larger groups.
sum.why: Covers the old view and the new evidence.

sum.t: A 2019 study analysed CCTV footage from three countries.
sum.why: Only the method.

sum.t: The bystander effect has been proved false, and every person in a crowd will help a stranger in trouble.
sum.why: At least one person usually helps; that is not everyone.

sum.t: Real footage confirmed that people in large crowds rarely step in to help.
sum.why: The footage showed the opposite.

s: In September 1666 a fire that began in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane burned for four days across the City of London.
It destroyed more than thirteen thousand houses, along with old St Paul's Cathedral and dozens of parish churches.
The disaster spread so easily because most buildings were made of timber and stood close together on narrow streets.
The rebuilding laws that followed therefore required new houses to be built of brick or stone, and some streets were widened.
marks: It destroyed more than thirteen thousand houses
The rebuilding laws that followed therefore
cues: Gives the event and the date, so it opens.
'It' is the fire.
'The disaster' sums up the destruction, and the sentence explains it.
'Therefore' draws on the timber buildings just blamed.
odd: London's population grew rapidly in the eighteenth century, making it one of Europe's largest cities.
oddWhy: It is about later growth, not about the fire and the rules that followed it.
ins: Grand plans for a new street layout, including one by Christopher Wren, were never carried out.
insWhy: It adds what did not happen in the rebuilding, so it follows the new laws; putting it earlier would cut 'therefore' off from its reason.

sum.t: The Great Fire of 1666 spread through London's crowded timber buildings, so the city was rebuilt under rules requiring brick or stone.
sum.why: Covers the fire, its cause and the response.

sum.t: The fire of 1666 began in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane.
sum.why: Only the start of the fire.

sum.t: After 1666, London was rebuilt to an entirely new plan by Christopher Wren, with wide streets everywhere and no timber buildings left anywhere in the city.
sum.why: Only some streets were widened, and the new street plans, including Wren's, were not carried out.

sum.t: Fires were the main cause of death in seventeenth-century London.
sum.why: Causes of death are not discussed.

s: In the 1960s India faced repeated food shortages and depended heavily on imported grain.
New high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, grown with irrigation and chemical fertiliser, changed this within a decade, above all in Punjab and Haryana.
This Green Revolution made the country largely self-sufficient in food grains, but it came at a price.
Farmers in those states now pump groundwater far faster than rain can replace it, and the water table in many districts falls year after year.
cues: Sets out the problem, so it opens.
'Changed this' refers to the shortages.
'This Green Revolution' names the change just described.
'Those states' are Punjab and Haryana, and the sentence gives the price.
odd: Rice is the staple food of most people in eastern and southern India.
oddWhy: It is about diets in other regions, not about the costs of the Green Revolution.
ins: Rice, which needs far more water than the crops it often replaced, has made the problem worse.
insWhy: 'The problem' is the falling water table, which is described only in the last sentence.

sum.t: High-yielding crops ended India's dependence on grain imports, but they have drained groundwater where they are grown most.
sum.why: Covers the gain and its cost.

sum.t: Farmers in Punjab pump groundwater faster than rain replaces it.
sum.why: Only the cost, without the gain.

sum.t: The Green Revolution failed, because India still depends on imported grain.
sum.why: It made India largely self-sufficient.

sum.t: Chemical fertiliser and irrigation should be banned in Punjab and Haryana to save their water, even if India must import grain again.
sum.why: No policy is recommended.

s: In a well-known 1973 experiment, psychologists observed nursery-school children who already liked drawing with felt-tip pens.
Some of the children were promised a certificate for drawing, while others were not.
A week or two later, the children who had been rewarded spent less of their free time drawing than those who had not.
The researchers concluded that an expected reward can turn an activity people enjoy into something they do mainly for the prize.
marks: Some of the children were promised
cues: Introduces the experiment, so it opens.
'The children' are the ones just introduced.
'Later' follows the reward, and the sentence gives the result.
The conclusion follows the result it explains.
odd: Drawing is widely thought to help young children develop fine control of their hands.
oddWhy: It is about drawing and development, not about rewards reducing interest.
ins: The certificate was shown to them before they began, so they knew exactly what they were drawing for.
insWhy: 'The certificate' needs the promise in the second sentence, and the children see it before the later result.

sum.t: Children promised a reward for drawing later drew less in their free time, suggesting expected rewards can undermine enjoyment.
sum.why: Covers the result and the conclusion.

sum.t: Some nursery-school children were promised a certificate for drawing.
sum.why: Only the set-up.

sum.t: Rewards always destroy interest in any activity, so parents and schools should never offer prizes.
sum.why: The paragraph says expected rewards 'can' do this, and gives no advice.

sum.t: The rewarded children enjoyed drawing more and spent more of their free time on it.
sum.why: They spent less time drawing.

s: Many bats find their way and catch insects in complete darkness by using sound.
They send out rapid, high-pitched calls, most of them too high for human ears, and listen for the echoes that bounce back.
From the timing and pattern of these echoes, a bat can judge the distance, size and even texture of objects around it.
This skill, called echolocation, was first demonstrated by the American scientist Donald Griffin in the late 1930s and 1940s.
marks: From the timing and pattern of these echoes
cues: States the general fact, so it opens.
'They' are the bats, and the sentence explains how sound is used.
'These echoes' are the ones just mentioned.
'This skill' sums up the process and names it.
odd: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight.
oddWhy: It is about flight, not about finding the way by sound.
ins: Before then, many scientists had refused to believe that animals could find their way by sound alone.
insWhy: 'Before then' needs the date of Griffin's work in the last sentence.

sum.t: Bats navigate and hunt in darkness by reading the echoes of their calls, an ability first shown in the twentieth century.
sum.why: Covers what bats do, how, and when it was shown.

sum.t: Bat calls are mostly too high for humans to hear.
sum.why: Only one detail.

sum.t: All bats are blind and depend entirely on sound to survive.
sum.why: The paragraph says 'many bats' use sound, and nothing says they are blind.

sum.t: Bats judge the distance and size of objects by listening to the calls of other bats flying nearby, rather than to the echoes of their own.
sum.why: They listen to the echoes of their own calls.

s: The Library of Alexandria is often remembered as having vanished in a single great fire.
Popular accounts blame Julius Caesar, a Christian mob or an Arab conqueror, depending on who tells the story.
Most historians think the truth was less dramatic.
The library seems to have declined over several centuries, as royal funding dried up, scholars left and the city suffered repeated wars.
marks: seems to have declined over several centuries
cues: States the popular memory, so it opens.
Lists the culprits of the single-fire story.
'Less dramatic' contrasts with the stories just told.
Spells out the less dramatic truth.
odd: Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in the fourth century BCE.
oddWhy: It is about the city's founding, not about how the library was lost.
ins: The story of one catastrophe survives because it makes a better tale than a slow loss of money and staff.
insWhy: 'A slow loss of money and staff' needs the decline described in the last sentence.

sum.t: The Library of Alexandria probably faded slowly through neglect and war, not in the single fire of popular legend.
sum.why: Covers the legend and the historians' view.

sum.t: Some accounts blame Julius Caesar for burning the library.
sum.why: Only one version of the legend.

sum.t: Historians agree that an Arab conqueror burned the library in a single night, ending centuries of scholarship at a stroke.
sum.why: Historians reject the single-fire story.

sum.t: The library never existed, and every story about it is a legend.
sum.why: The paragraph is about how it declined, not whether it existed.

s: In 1817 the economist David Ricardo set out an argument that still surprises students.
He imagined England and Portugal producing cloth and wine, with Portugal better at making both.
Even so, he showed, both countries gain if each specialises in what it makes relatively best and trades for the rest.
What matters for trade, in other words, is not absolute advantage but comparative advantage: what a country gives up by making one good rather than another.
marks: David Ricardo set out an argument
cues: Introduces Ricardo, so it opens.
'He' is Ricardo, and the sentence sets up his example.
'Even so' answers Portugal being better at both.
'In other words' restates the result as a general principle.
odd: Portugal has been famous for its port wine since the eighteenth century.
oddWhy: It is about Portuguese wine, not about Ricardo's argument.
ins: It might seem that Portugal would have no reason to buy anything from England.
insWhy: It draws the obvious conclusion from Portugal being better at both, which 'Even so' then overturns.

sum.t: Ricardo showed that countries gain by specialising where their relative costs are lowest, even when one is better at everything.
sum.why: Covers the example's point and the principle.

sum.t: Ricardo used England and Portugal as an example in 1817.
sum.why: Only the set-up.

sum.t: Ricardo argued that a country should trade only if it is better than others at making something.
sum.why: That is absolute advantage, which he showed does not matter.

sum.t: Free trade makes every country and every worker better off, which is why all economists, following Ricardo, have supported it since 1817.
sum.why: The paragraph makes no claim about every worker or all economists.

s: Tardigrades are animals less than a millimetre long that live in moss, soil and water almost everywhere on Earth.
They are famous for surviving conditions that would kill nearly any other animal, from near-total drying to the vacuum of space.
They manage this by entering a state called a tun, in which they lose almost all their water and their metabolism nearly stops.
In their normal active state, however, tardigrades are far more fragile, and many die from heat or drought that strikes too quickly for them to prepare.
marks: In their normal active state, however
cues: Introduces tardigrades, so it opens.
'They' are tardigrades, and the sentence gives their fame.
'This' is surviving the extremes just listed.
'However' turns from the tough tun state to the fragile active one.
odd: Some species of moss can also survive for years without water.
oddWhy: It is about moss, not about tardigrades.
ins: That claim rests on a 2007 experiment in which tardigrades were carried into orbit and exposed to open space, and some survived.
insWhy: 'That claim' is the claim about surviving space, so it follows it, before the explanation of how they survive.

sum.t: Tardigrades survive extremes by drying into a dormant state, but when active they are much more fragile.
sum.why: Covers their toughness, how it works and its limit.

sum.t: Tardigrades live in moss, soil and water.
sum.why: Only where they live.

sum.t: Tardigrades cannot be killed by any conditions on Earth or in space, which is why they live almost everywhere on the planet.
sum.why: Active tardigrades die easily.

sum.t: Tardigrades are strongest when active and become fragile only after they dry out.
sum.why: It is the other way round.

s: In the 1780s the philosopher Jeremy Bentham designed a prison he called the Panopticon.
Its cells were arranged in a ring around a central tower, from which a guard could look into any cell without being seen.
Because prisoners could never tell whether they were being watched, Bentham expected them to behave as if they always were.
Two centuries later, the philosopher Michel Foucault used the design as an image of modern society, in which people discipline themselves under the possibility of constant observation.
cues: Introduces the design, so it opens.
'Its cells' are the prison's.
Draws the effect of the unseen guard just described.
'Two centuries later' counts from Bentham's design.
odd: Bentham also argued that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
oddWhy: It is about Bentham's ethics, not about the prison design and its meaning.
ins: The guard, in other words, need hardly watch at all; the prisoners would do the work themselves.
insWhy: 'In other words' restates Bentham's expectation just given, before the paragraph moves on to Foucault.

sum.t: Bentham's prison relied on inmates never knowing if they were watched, an idea Foucault later applied to society as a whole.
sum.why: Covers the design, its logic and Foucault's use of it.

sum.t: The Panopticon's cells were arranged in a ring around a tower.
sum.why: Only the layout.

sum.t: Foucault praised the Panopticon as a humane model for running modern prisons.
sum.why: Foucault used it as an image of society, not as a model prison.

sum.t: Modern society is a prison in which every person is watched by the government at all times, exactly as Bentham planned in the 1780s.
sum.why: The paragraph speaks of the possibility of observation, not constant government watching.

s: The idea of moving clocks forward in summer to make better use of daylight was proposed long before any country adopted it.
Germany and Austria-Hungary were the first to do so nationally, in 1916, hoping to save coal for the war effort.
Britain and many other countries soon followed, and the practice has been kept, dropped and revived many times since.
Today its value is disputed: studies find the energy savings small or uncertain, while the twice-yearly change in sleep has been linked to a brief rise in accidents.
marks: The idea of moving clocks forward
the first to do so nationally
Britain and many other countries soon followed
cues: Introduces the idea, so it opens.
'To do so' is adopting the idea just introduced.
'Soon followed' needs the first countries named.
'Today' brings the history up to the present debate.
odd: Railway companies in the nineteenth century pushed for standard time zones so that timetables would make sense.
oddWhy: It is about time zones, not about summer clock changes.
ins: Benjamin Franklin joked in 1784 that Parisians could save candles simply by getting up earlier.
insWhy: It shows how early the idea appeared, so it follows the first sentence and comes before the first adoption in 1916.

sum.t: First adopted nationally in wartime to save fuel, daylight saving time spread widely, but its benefits are now in doubt.
sum.why: Covers its origin, spread and the present dispute.

sum.t: Germany adopted daylight saving time in 1916 to save coal.
sum.why: Only the first adoption.

sum.t: Studies have shown that daylight saving time wastes energy and causes most road accidents in the weeks after the clocks change.
sum.why: Studies find small or uncertain savings and a brief rise in accidents.

sum.t: Every country should abolish daylight saving time immediately.
sum.why: No advice is given.

s: The cities of the Indus Valley, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, flourished more than four thousand years ago with planned streets, drains and standard weights.
Their people left thousands of short inscriptions on seals, pottery and tablets.
Yet the script remains undeciphered, despite a century of attempts.
The inscriptions are very brief, no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone has been found, and the language they record is unknown.
marks: The cities of the Indus Valley
cues: Introduces the cities, so it opens.
'Their people' are the cities' inhabitants.
'Yet' sets the failure against the many inscriptions.
Gives the reasons the script is still unread.
odd: Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath is one of the earliest known public water tanks.
oddWhy: It is about a building, not about the script.
ins: Without such a key, every proposed decipherment has been impossible to test.
insWhy: 'Such a key' is the bilingual text mentioned in the last sentence.

sum.t: The Indus script stays unread: its texts are short, no bilingual exists, and its language is unknown.
sum.why: Covers the failure and its reasons.

sum.t: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had planned streets and drains.
sum.why: Only the background.

sum.t: The Indus script can never be deciphered by anyone, whatever new evidence is found.
sum.why: The paragraph explains why it is hard, not that it is impossible.

sum.t: Scholars can read the Indus inscriptions on seals and pottery but still cannot agree on which language lies behind them.
sum.why: The script is undeciphered.

s: In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup devised a simple test of whether animals recognise themselves.
He placed a mark on a chimpanzee's face where it could be seen only in a mirror, and watched whether the animal touched the mark on its own body.
Chimpanzees did, and so, in later studies, did a few other species, including orangutans, some dolphins and magpies.
Critics point out, however, that the test favours animals that rely on sight, and that failing it may not mean an animal lacks a sense of self.
marks: Gordon Gallup devised a simple test
cues: Introduces the test, so it opens.
'He' is Gallup, and the sentence describes the test.
'Did' answers whether the animal touched the mark.
'However' turns from the results to their limits.
odd: Mirrors made of polished metal were used in ancient Egypt and China.
oddWhy: It is about the history of mirrors, not about animals recognising themselves.
ins: Monkeys, by contrast, generally treated the reflection as another animal.
insWhy: 'By contrast' needs the species that passed, so it follows them, before the criticism.

sum.t: The mirror test suggests a few species recognise themselves, though critics say it favours sight and failure proves little.
sum.why: Covers the test, its results and the criticism.

sum.t: Gallup put a mark on a chimpanzee's face in 1970.
sum.why: Only the method.

sum.t: Only chimpanzees have a sense of self, as the mirror test proves.
sum.why: Other species passed, and critics doubt what failing shows.

sum.t: Critics argue that the mirror test is too easy, so animals that pass it may not really recognise themselves.
sum.why: Critics say failing it may not show a lack of self.
